claim: IFIT proteins are critical mediators of mammalian innate antiviral immunity.
source: IFIT (interferon-induced with tetratricopeptide repeats) proteins are critical mediators of mammalian innate antiviral immunity.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader literature and the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mouse IFIT1 selectively inhibits viruses that lack 2'O-methylation of their mRNA 5' caps.
source: Mouse IFIT1 selectively inhibits viruses that lack 2'O-methylation of their mRNA 5' caps.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work (Daffis et al., 2010; Hyde et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2014; Menachery et al., 2014; Szretter et al., 2012; Zust et al., 2011; Habjan et al., 2013; Kimura et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2014) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Human IFIT1 does not share the antiviral specificity of mouse IFIT1 for cap0-mRNA.
source: Surprisingly, human IFIT1 does not share this antiviral specificity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Andrejeva et al., 2013; Pichlmair et al., 2011; Pinto et al., 2015) and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Human IFIT1 and mouse IFIT1 (renamed IFIT1B) are not orthologs, but are paralogs that diverged >100 mya.
source: First, we show that human IFIT1 and mouse IFIT1 (renamed IFIT1B) are not orthologs, but are paralogs that diverged >100 mya.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses presented in Figures 1, 2, and 3, showing the evolutionary relationships of IFIT genes.

claim: IFIT1 and IFIT1B proteins differ in their ability to be suppressed by a cap 2'O-methyltransferase.
source: Second, using a yeast genetic assay, we show that IFIT1 and IFIT1B proteins differ in their ability to be suppressed by a cap 2'O-methyltransferase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assays shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Only IFIT1 proteins inhibit a virus encoding a cap 2'O-methyltransferase.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that IFIT1 and IFIT1B have divergent antiviral specificities, including the discovery that only IFIT1 proteins inhibit a virus encoding a cap 2'O-methyltransferase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the VSV infection experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: There is widespread turnover of mammalian IFIT genes.
source: These functional data, combined with widespread turnover of mammalian IFIT genes, reveal dramatic species-specific differences in IFIT-mediated antiviral repertoires.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Humans have five intact IFIT genes (IFIT1, 1B, 2, 3 and 5).
source: For instance, while humans have five intact IFIT genes (IFIT1, 1B, 2, 3 and 5), rats have four (IFIT1, 1b, 2 and 3) and mice have six (IFIT1, 1b, 1c, 2, 3 and 3b) (Fensterl and Sen, 2011; 2015; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Fensterl and Sen, 2011; 2015; Liu et al., 2013) and genomic analyses.

claim: Rats have four intact IFIT genes (IFIT1, 1b, 2 and 3).
source: For instance, while humans have five intact IFIT genes (IFIT1, 1B, 2, 3 and 5), rats have four (IFIT1, 1b, 2 and 3) and mice have six (IFIT1, 1b, 1c, 2, 3 and 3b) (Fensterl and Sen, 2011; 2015; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Fensterl and Sen, 2011; 2015; Liu et al., 2013) and genomic analyses.

claim: Mice have six intact IFIT genes (IFIT1, 1b, 1c, 2, 3 and 3b).
source: For instance, while humans have five intact IFIT genes (IFIT1, 1B, 2, 3 and 5), rats have four (IFIT1, 1b, 2 and 3) and mice have six (IFIT1, 1b, 1c, 2, 3 and 3b) (Fensterl and Sen, 2011; 2015; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Fensterl and Sen, 2011; 2015; Liu et al., 2013) and genomic analyses.

claim: IFIT1 and IFIT2 from humans and mice inhibit mRNA translation through interactions with the translation initiation factor eIF3.
source: Initial studies with IFIT1 and IFIT2 from humans and mice indicated that these proteins might mediate their antiviral activity by inhibiting mRNA translation through interactions with the translation initiation factor eIF3 (Guo et al., 2000; Hui et al., 2003; Terenzi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Guo et al., 2000; Hui et al., 2003; Terenzi et al., 2005).

claim: PKR recognizes cytoplasmic double-stranded RNA and triggers global repression of protein synthesis.
source: In the case of PKR, the recognition of cytoplasmic double-stranded RNA, a by-product of viral replication, triggers its activity and the global repression of protein synthesis (Dever et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Dever et al., 2007).

claim: During mammalian mRNA processing, the 5' cap region is 2'O-methylated from a cap0-structure to a cap1-structure.
source: During mammalian mRNA processing, the 5' cap region is 2'O-methylated from a cap0-structure (7mGpppN, where 7mG is the 7-methyl guanosine, ppp is the triphosphate linkage, and N is any nucleotide) to a cap1-structure (7mGpppNm) (Banerjee, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Banerjee, 1980).

claim: The 2'O-methylation reaction is catalyzed in the host nucleus by a dedicated 2'O-methyltransferase, known as a cap1-methyltransferase (hCMTR1 in humans).
source: This reaction is catalyzed in the host nucleus by a dedicated 2'O-methyltransferase, known as a cap1-methyltransferase (hCMTR1 in humans) (Belanger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Belanger et al., 2010).

claim: Many viruses have evolved ways to mimic host cap1-structures.
source: Interestingly, many viruses have evolved ways to mimic host cap1-structures (Banerjee, 1980; Decroly et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Banerjee, 1980; Decroly et al., 2012).

claim: Poxviruses, flaviviruses, coronaviruses, and rhabdoviruses produce cap1-mRNAs by encoding a virally-encoded cap1-methyltransferase.
source: For several viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm, such as poxviruses, flaviviruses, coronaviruses, and rhabdoviruses, 2'O-methylation of the cap is catalyzed by a virally-encoded cap1-methyltransferase.
evidence: This is supported by general knowledge of viral biology and citations mentioned elsewhere in the manuscript (Banerjee, 1980; Decroly et al., 2012).

claim: Orthomyxoviruses, arenaviruses, and bunyaviruses produce cap1-mRNAs by 'cap-snatching'.
source: For other viruses, such as orthomyxoviruses, arenaviruses, and bunyaviruses, the effect is achieved by 'cap-snatching', in which a segment of cap1-modified host mRNA is appended to viral mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by general knowledge of viral biology and citations mentioned elsewhere in the manuscript (Banerjee, 1980; Decroly et al., 2012).

claim: Mouse IFIT1 inhibits replication of numerous viruses naturally lacking or mutated to lack 2'O-methylation by directly binding and inhibiting translation of cap0-mRNAs.
source: Indeed, mouse IFIT1 was discovered to inhibit replication of numerous viruses naturally lacking or mutated to lack 2'O-methylation by directly binding and inhibiting translation of cap0-mRNAs (Daffis et al., 2010; Hyde et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2014; Menachery et al., 2014; Szretter et al., 2012; Zust et al., 2011; Habjan et al., 2013; Kimura et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies (Daffis et al., 2010; Hyde et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2014; Menachery et al., 2014; Szretter et al., 2012; Zust et al., 2011; Habjan et al., 2013; Kimura et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2014).

claim: Human IFIT1 inhibits mRNA translation and replication of parainfluenza virus 5 (PIV5), despite the fact that PIV5 encodes a cap1-methyltransferase.
source: For instance, human IFIT1 was shown to inhibit mRNA translation and replication of parainfluenza virus 5 (PIV5), despite the fact that PIV5 encodes a cap1-methyltransferase and PIV5 mRNAs are 2'O-methylated on their caps (Andrejeva et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Andrejeva et al., 2013).

claim: Human IFIT1 has been implicated in inhibition of hepatitis C virus (HCV).
source: Other studies have implicated human IFIT1 in inhibition of hepatitis C virus (HCV) (Raychoudhuri et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2003), human papillomavirus (HPV) (Terenzi et al., 2008), influenza A virus (IAV) and vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) (Pichlmair et al., 2011), none of which are predicted to translate proteins from cap0-mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Raychoudhuri et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2003).

claim: Human IFIT1 has been implicated in inhibition of human papillomavirus (HPV).
source: Other studies have implicated human IFIT1 in inhibition of hepatitis C virus (HCV) (Raychoudhuri et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2003), human papillomavirus (HPV) (Terenzi et al., 2008), influenza A virus (IAV) and vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) (Pichlmair et al., 2011), none of which are predicted to translate proteins from cap0-mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Terenzi et al., 2008).

claim: Human IFIT1 has been implicated in inhibition of influenza A virus (IAV) and vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV).
source: Other studies have implicated human IFIT1 in inhibition of hepatitis C virus (HCV) (Raychoudhuri et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2003), human papillomavirus (HPV) (Terenzi et al., 2008), influenza A virus (IAV) and vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) (Pichlmair et al., 2011), none of which are predicted to translate proteins from cap0-mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Pichlmair et al., 2011).

claim: HCV, HPV, IAV, and VSV are not predicted to translate proteins from cap0-mRNAs.
source: Other studies have implicated human IFIT1 in inhibition of hepatitis C virus (HCV) (Raychoudhuri et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2003), human papillomavirus (HPV) (Terenzi et al., 2008), influenza A virus (IAV) and vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) (Pichlmair et al., 2011), none of which are predicted to translate proteins from cap0-mRNAs.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of viral biology and the cap structures of these viruses.

claim: Mouse IFIT1 is more similar at the sequence level to human IFIT1B than to human IFIT1 (57% versus 53% pairwise amino acid identity).
source: Furthermore, mouse IFIT1 is more similar at the sequence level to another human IFIT, the poorly characterized human IFIT1B, than to human IFIT1 (57% versus 53% pairwise amino acid identity).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data.

claim: IFIT genes are located in a single locus in most mammalian species.
source: Our phylogenetic analyses were facilitated by the fact that IFIT genes are located in a single locus in most mammalian species (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Liu et al., 2013) and genomic data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Human chromosome 10 contains a single locus that encodes all five intact IFIT genes: IFIT1, IFIT1B, IFIT2, IFIT3 and IFIT5.
source: For example, human chromosome 10 contains a single locus that encodes all five intact IFIT genes: IFIT1, IFIT1B, IFIT2, IFIT3 and IFIT5 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The IFIT locus organization is similar in many mammalian genomes including African green monkeys, rabbits, cats, ferrets, and armadillos.
source: We found the IFIT locus organization is similar in many other mammalian genomes including African green monkeys, rabbits, cats, ferrets, and armadillos (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A single duplication of IFIT1 may have occurred early in mammalian evolution, before the radiation of placental mammals over 100 million years ago.
source: In this shared syntenic arrangement, two IFIT1 paralogs are found next to each other in the same sense orientation as IFIT2 and IFIT3, suggesting that a single duplication of IFIT1 may have occurred early in mammalian evolution, i.e., before the radiation of placental mammals over 100 million years ago.
evidence: This is inferred from the syntenic arrangement of IFIT genes across multiple mammalian species shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The IFIT locus in mice and rats is arranged quite differently than other mammalian genomes.
source: In contrast, the IFIT locus in mice and rats is arranged quite differently than other mammalian genomes.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mice have three IFIT1 paralogs, two of which are in the opposite orientation to IFIT2 and IFIT3.
source: Instead of two paralogs, mice have three IFIT1 paralogs, two of which are in the opposite orientation to IFIT2 and IFIT3 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IFIT2, IFIT3 and IFIT5 genes form distinct, monophyletic clades that diverged as expected based on known mammalian species evolution.
source: We found unambiguous phylogenetic signatures that delineate IFIT2, IFIT3 and IFIT5 genes into distinct, monophyletic clades that diverged as expected based on known mammalian species evolution (O'Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 1B and a citation to previous work (O'Leary et al., 2013).

claim: IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes could not be resolved into distinct clades in phylogenetic analyses using full-length gene sequences.
source: In contrast to these three gene families, we were unable to resolve IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes into distinct clades in our phylogenetic analyses.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There are several instances of IFIT1 and IFIT1B from the same species appearing more phylogenetically related to each other than to their similarly named genes from a sister species.
source: Instead, similar to previous studies (Liu, 2013), we found several instances of IFIT1 and IFIT1B from the same species (e.g., cat) appearing more phylogenetically related to each other than to their similarly named genes from a sister species (e.g., ferret) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 1B and a citation to a previous study (Liu, 2013).

claim: IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes have recurrently recombined with each other through gene conversion.
source: In this alternative, IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes duplicated early in mammalian evolution but have recurrently recombined with each other. Resulting gene conversion would scramble the phylogenetic relatedness of the two genes without altering their genomic locations.
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gene conversion has contributed to the evolution of several multigene families including mammalian interferon alpha genes.
source: Such gene conversion has been shown to contribute to the evolution of several multigene families including mammalian interferon alpha genes (Benovoy and Drouin, 2009; Hurles, 2004; Petronella and Drouin, 2011; Santoyo and Romero, 2005; Song et al., 2011; Woelk et al., 2007; Yasukochi and Satta, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Benovoy and Drouin, 2009; Hurles, 2004; Petronella and Drouin, 2011; Santoyo and Romero, 2005; Song et al., 2011; Woelk et al., 2007; Yasukochi and Satta, 2015).

claim: The sequences of IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes in cats are 86% identical at the whole gene level.
source: For example, the sequences of IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes in cats are 86% identical at the whole gene level.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cat IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes are 97% identical in the 5' ends of the genes (nucleotides 1–948 in cat IFIT1) but only 63% identical in the 3' ends of the genes.
source: However, these two genes are 97% identical in the 5' ends of the genes (nucleotides 1–948 in cat IFIT1) but only 63% identical in the 3' ends of the genes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The 5' ends of IFIT1 and IFIT1B underwent gene conversion recently in the evolution of the cat IFIT locus.
source: Such an uneven distribution of sequence differences strongly suggests that the 5' ends of IFIT1 and IFIT1B underwent gene conversion recently in the evolution of the cat IFIT locus, leading to sequence homogenization of the first two-thirds of the gene.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Between ferret IFIT1 and IFIT1B, the 5' ends are 98% identical, but 3' ends are only 62% identical.
source: For instance, between ferret IFIT1 and IFIT1B, the 5' ends are 98% identical, but 3' ends are only 62% identical (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A similar dichotomy in sequence identity is evident in a comparison between rabbit IFIT1 and IFIT1B and between armadillo IFIT1 and IFIT1B.
source: A similar dichotomy is evident in a comparison between rabbit IFIT1 and IFIT1B and between armadillo IFIT1 and IFIT1B (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: All gene conversion events between IFIT1 and IFIT1B have a similar recurrent breakpoint approximately two-thirds of the way through the gene sequence.
source: Interestingly, all of these gene conversion events have a similar recurrent breakpoint approximately two-thirds of the way through the gene sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) that maps to a 'pivot' point between subdomains in the homologous IFIT5 structure (Abbas et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and structural mapping shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, with a citation to previous work (Abbas et al., 2013).

claim: The recombination breakpoint maps to a 'pivot' point between subdomains in the homologous IFIT5 structure.
source: Interestingly, all of these gene conversion events have a similar recurrent breakpoint approximately two-thirds of the way through the gene sequence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) that maps to a 'pivot' point between subdomains in the homologous IFIT5 structure (Abbas et al., 2013) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on structural mapping shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and a citation to previous work (Abbas et al., 2013).

claim: Recurrent gene conversion has confounded the phylogenetic relationships of the 5' segment of IFIT1 and IFIT1B.
source: Thus, our findings suggest that recurrent gene conversion has confounded the phylogenetic relationships of the 5' segment of IFIT1 and IFIT1B, which likely do not accurately represent the actual ancestry of these genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence comparison and phylogenetic data shown in Figures 2 and 2—figure supplements.

claim: IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes cluster into distinct monophyletic clades when using only the 3' end of the gene alignment.
source: In contrast to the analyses using the full-length IFIT genes (Figure 1B) or the 5' end of the IFIT genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), we now discern clear separation of IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes. Both IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes form distinct monophyletic clades that diverge according to mammalian species evolution, similar to other IFIT genes.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2C.

claim: IFIT1 and IFIT1B duplicated early in mammalian evolution.
source: Based on this phylogenetic concordance, as well as the agreement with synteny data, we infer that this phylogeny reflects the actual ancestry of IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes in mammals. Importantly, these data indicate that IFIT1 and IFIT1B duplicated early in mammalian evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2C and synteny data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Following the IFIT1/IFIT1B duplication, the 3' ends of the two genes have been diverging according to speciation events, whereas the 5' ends have recurrently recombined.
source: Following this duplication, the 3' ends of the two genes have been diverging according to speciation events, whereas the 5' ends have recurrently recombined.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic and sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: All three mouse IFIT1 paralogs (previously named mouse IFIT1, IFIT1b and IFIT1c) and both rat paralogs (previously named rat IFIT1 and IFIT1b) unambiguously group within the IFIT1B gene family.
source: These data also reveal that all three mouse IFIT1 paralogs (previously named mouse IFIT1, IFIT1b and IFIT1c) and both rat paralogs (previously named rat IFIT1 and IFIT1b) unambiguously group within the IFIT1B gene family.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mouse and rat have lost all copies of IFIT1, likely through a deletion of both IFIT1 and the neighboring IFIT5.
source: We, therefore, infer that mouse and rat have lost all copies of IFIT1, likely through a deletion of both IFIT1 and the neighboring IFIT5.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2C and genomic data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mouse and rat genomes now bear recently duplicated copies of IFIT1B.
source: Instead, mouse and rat genomes now bear recently duplicated copies of IFIT1B.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2C and genomic data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Most placental mammals contain members of the IFIT1, 1B, 2, 3 and 5 gene families.
source: We found that most placental mammals contain members of the IFIT1, 1B, 2, 3 and 5 gene families (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Marsupials encode a more limited set of IFIT genes including a single gene that predates the IFIT2/IFIT3 duplication and a single gene that predates IFIT1/IFIT1B divergence.
source: In contrast, marsupials encode a more limited set of IFIT genes including a single gene that predates the IFIT2/IFIT3 duplication and a single gene that predates IFIT1/IFIT1B divergence (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The human-like IFIT repertoire (IFIT1, 1B, 2, 3 and 5) was established when placental mammals diverged from non-placental mammals approximately 100–200 mya.
source: Based on these analyses, we infer that the human-like IFIT repertoire (IFIT1, 1B, 2, 3 and 5) was established when placental mammals diverged from non-placental mammals approximately 100–200 mya while other vertebrates have undergone lineage-specific expansions of IFITs.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: GARD and SBP analyses found strong statistical support for a recombination breakpoint approximately two-thirds of the way through the IFIT gene sequence.
source: Both analyses found strong statistical support (GARD p-value <0.001, SBP 100% model averaged support) for a recombination breakpoint approximately two-thirds of the way through the IFIT gene sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on GARD and SBP analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is no evidence for additional recombination breakpoints in the 3' region of the IFIT alignment.
source: Importantly, performing the same analyses for the 3' region of the IFIT alignment found no evidence for additional recombination breakpoints (GARD p-value >0.1, SBP 0% model averaged support), supporting the assertion that these regions have not recombined during mammalian IFIT evolution.
evidence: This is based on GARD and SBP analyses.

claim: IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes cluster into distinct monophyletic clades when using the non-recombining 3' region of vertebrate IFITs.
source: Indeed, construction of a phylogenetic tree of this non-recombining region of vertebrate IFITs shows that IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes cluster into distinct monophyletic clades (Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and supplement 3.

claim: There are at least five separate cases of gene conversion between IFIT1 and IFIT1B in the carnivores.
source: In contrast, a phylogenetic tree created from just the 5' end of vertebrate IFITs reveals numerous instances of gene conversion, including at least five separate cases in the carnivores alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: All primates encode an intact IFIT1.
source: For instance, in primates, we found that IFIT1 and IFIT1B genes have diverged as expected based on primate phylogeny and that all primates encode an intact IFIT1.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: IFIT1B has been pseudogenized at least twice in the primate lineage as the result of the introduction of nonsense codons and frameshift mutations, once in chimpanzees and again in both sequenced New World monkeys.
source: In contrast, we found that IFIT1B has been pseudogenized at least twice in the primate lineage as the result of the introduction of nonsense codons and frameshift mutations, once in chimpanzees and again in both sequenced New World monkeys (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and supplement 4.

claim: There is evidence for at least seven independent instances of IFIT1B loss across 51 sampled vertebrate species.
source: In total, we found evidence for at least seven independent instances of IFIT1B loss, two separate instances of IFIT1 loss, and at least 13 independent instances of IFIT1/1B gene conversion.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and genomic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is evidence for two separate instances of IFIT1 loss across 51 sampled vertebrate species.
source: In total, we found evidence for at least seven independent instances of IFIT1B loss, two separate instances of IFIT1 loss, and at least 13 independent instances of IFIT1/1B gene conversion.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and genomic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is evidence for at least 13 independent instances of IFIT1/1B gene conversion across 51 sampled vertebrate species.
source: In total, we found evidence for at least seven independent instances of IFIT1B loss, two separate instances of IFIT1 loss, and at least 13 independent instances of IFIT1/1B gene conversion.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and genomic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: Most changes in the gene repertoire of IFITs across mammalian species are focused on IFIT1 and IFIT1B.
source: Interestingly, it appears that most changes in the gene repertoire of IFITs across mammalian species are focused on IFIT1 and IFIT1B, although there are also instances of lineage-specific gene births and loss in other IFIT genes as well.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and genomic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: IFIT3 has duplicated in mice.
source: For example, IFIT3 has duplicated in mice, whereas IFIT5 has been lost in several rodents (which may have occurred coincident with IFIT1 loss).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and genomic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: IFIT5 has been lost in several rodents.
source: For example, IFIT3 has duplicated in mice, whereas IFIT5 has been lost in several rodents (which may have occurred coincident with IFIT1 loss).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic and genomic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: The loss of IFIT5 in rodents may have occurred coincident with IFIT1 loss.
source: For example, IFIT3 has duplicated in mice, whereas IFIT5 has been lost in several rodents (which may have occurred coincident with IFIT1 loss).
evidence: This is speculated based on the genomic arrangement of IFIT genes.

claim: Budding yeast mRNAs only have cap0-structures due to a lack of a cap1-methyltransferase.
source: To this end, we turned to the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, whose mRNAs only have cap0-structures (Banerjee, 1980) due to a lack of a cap1-methyltransferase.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Banerjee, 1980) and is established knowledge.

claim: Expression of mouse IFIT1B potently inhibits yeast growth.
source: Indeed, using a galactose-induced IFIT1B expression system, we found that expression of mouse IFIT1B potently inhibits yeast growth (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mouse IFIT1B does not require any other mammalian-specific cofactor to inhibit yeast growth.
source: Importantly, this growth inhibition occurs in the absence of any other IFIT or component of the innate immune system, indicating that mouse IFIT1B does not require any other mammalian-specific cofactor to perform this function.
evidence: This is inferred from the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 4B, where only mouse IFIT1B is expressed.

claim: Co-expression of the human cap1-methyltransferase (hCMTR1) nearly completely rescues yeast growth inhibited by mouse IFIT1B.
source: Strikingly, we observed nearly complete rescue of yeast growth when we co-expressed the human cap1-methyltransferase (hCMTR1), but not a catalytic mutant of hCMTR1 (K239A) (Belanger et al., 2010) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 4D, with a citation to previous work (Belanger et al., 2010) describing the catalytic mutant.

claim: A catalytic mutant of hCMTR1 (K239A) does not rescue yeast growth inhibited by mouse IFIT1B.
source: Strikingly, we observed nearly complete rescue of yeast growth when we co-expressed the human cap1-methyltransferase (hCMTR1), but not a catalytic mutant of hCMTR1 (K239A) (Belanger et al., 2010) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 4D, with a citation to previous work (Belanger et al., 2010) describing the catalytic mutant.

claim: Mouse IFIT1B-mediated growth inhibition of budding yeast is specifically due to the lack of a functional cap1-methyltransferase in yeast.
source: We, therefore, conclude that the mouse IFIT1B-mediated growth inhibition of budding yeast is specifically due to the lack of a functional cap1-methyltransferase in yeast, accurately recapitulating the known antiviral molecular specificity of IFIT1B (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is concluded from the yeast growth assays shown in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: Gibbon and African green monkey (AGM) IFIT1B cause robust growth inhibition of yeast that can be rescued by expression of hCMTR1.
source: Consistent with our phylogenetic prediction, we observed robust growth inhibition as a result of expression of gibbon and African green monkey (AGM) IFIT1B that could be rescued by expression of hCMTR1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Human IFIT1B does not cause growth inhibition of yeast.
source: Surprisingly, we observed no growth inhibition by human IFIT1B.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Human IFIT1B lacks function.
source: This lack of activity even upon equivalent expression in yeast (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) is unusual among intact primate IFIT1Bs, suggesting that human IFIT1B lacks function. This result is consistent with previous suggestions (Fensterl and Sen, 2011) that human IFIT1B may be non-functional even though it appears to be encoded by an intact open reading frame.
evidence: This is inferred from the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 4E and protein expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with a citation to previous work (Fensterl and Sen, 2011).

claim: Expression of human IFIT1 results in a potent inhibition of yeast growth.
source: Similar to mouse IFIT1B, we found that expression of human IFIT1 resulted in a potent inhibition of yeast growth (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Overexpression of hCMTR1 does not rescue human IFIT1-mediated growth inhibition of yeast.
source: However, in contrast to mouse IFIT1B, we observed no rescue of human IFIT1-mediated growth inhibition upon overexpression of hCMTR1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 5B.

claim: IFIT1 proteins from gibbon and African Green Monkey (AGM) recapitulate the findings from human IFIT1 in yeast growth assays.
source: IFIT1 proteins from gibbon and African Green Monkey (AGM) recapitulate the findings from human IFIT1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IFIT1 proteins do not distinguish between absence or presence of a cap1-methyltransferase.
source: These data indicate that IFIT1 proteins do not distinguish between absence or presence of a cap1-methyltransferase (Figure 5D) but instead, likely recognize another as-yet-undefined 'non-self' molecular pattern, other than Cap0-mRNA, which is present in yeast.
evidence: This is concluded from the yeast growth assays shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: IFIT1 proteins likely recognize another as-yet-undefined 'non-self' molecular pattern, other than Cap0-mRNA, which is present in yeast.
source: These data indicate that IFIT1 proteins do not distinguish between absence or presence of a cap1-methyltransferase (Figure 5D) but instead, likely recognize another as-yet-undefined 'non-self' molecular pattern, other than Cap0-mRNA, which is present in yeast.
evidence: This is speculated based on the yeast growth assays shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: Cat IFIT1 and IFIT1B are 96% identical at the amino acid level in the N-terminus of the protein whereas the C-terminus is only 46% identical.
source: Cat IFIT1 and IFIT1B are 96% identical at the amino acid level in the N-terminus of the protein whereas the C-terminus is only 46% identical (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Both cat IFIT1 and IFIT1B are capable of causing growth inhibition of yeast.
source: Upon overexpression in yeast, both cat IFIT1 and IFIT1B were capable of causing growth inhibition (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Only inhibition by cat IFIT1B is rescued by hCMTR1.
source: However, only inhibition by cat IFIT1B was rescued by hCMTR1, suggesting that the C-terminus of the IFIT1 paralogs is critical for the differences in the molecular specificity of these two proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The C-terminus of the IFIT1 paralogs is critical for the differences in the molecular specificity of IFIT1 and IFIT1B.
source: However, only inhibition by cat IFIT1B was rescued by hCMTR1, suggesting that the C-terminus of the IFIT1 paralogs is critical for the differences in the molecular specificity of these two proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the yeast growth assay shown in Figure 5F.

claim: IFIT1 and IFIT1B gene families perform distinct molecular functions in the species in which they are found.
source: We, therefore, conclude that IFIT1 and IFIT1B gene families perform distinct molecular functions in the species in which they are found and that recurrent gene conversion of the N-termini of IFIT1/IFIT1B genes in mammals has not led to a loss of their separate functions.
evidence: This is concluded from the yeast growth assays shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Recurrent gene conversion of the N-termini of IFIT1/IFIT1B genes in mammals has not led to a loss of their separate functions.
source: We, therefore, conclude that IFIT1 and IFIT1B gene families perform distinct molecular functions in the species in which they are found and that recurrent gene conversion of the N-termini of IFIT1/IFIT1B genes in mammals has not led to a loss of their separate functions.
evidence: This is concluded from the yeast growth assays shown in Figures 4 and 5, particularly the cat IFIT1/IFIT1B data in Figure 5F.

claim: Expression of mouse IFIT1B can potently inhibit replication of a mutant vaccinia virus that lacks cap1-methyltransferase activity.
source: Consistent with previous studies with these same viruses (Daffis et al., 2010), we found that expression of mouse IFIT1B can potently inhibit replication of a mutant vaccinia virus that lacks cap1-methyltransferase activity, but was unable to inhibit replication of wildtype vaccinia virus (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the vaccinia virus infection experiments shown in Figure 6C, with a citation to previous work (Daffis et al., 2010).

claim: Mouse IFIT1B is unable to inhibit replication of wildtype vaccinia virus.
source: Consistent with previous studies with these same viruses (Daffis et al., 2010), we found that expression of mouse IFIT1B can potently inhibit replication of a mutant vaccinia virus that lacks cap1-methyltransferase activity, but was unable to inhibit replication of wildtype vaccinia virus (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the vaccinia virus infection experiments shown in Figure 6C, with a citation to previous work (Daffis et al., 2010).

claim: Singular overexpression of mouse IFIT1B is sufficient for inhibition of viruses encoding cap0-mRNAs.
source: While the previous mouse knockout experiment had demonstrated that mouse IFIT1B is necessary for inhibition of viruses encoding cap0-mRNAs (Daffis et al., 2010), our findings show that singular overexpression of mouse IFIT1B is also sufficient for such inhibition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the vaccinia virus infection experiments shown in Figure 6C, with a citation to previous work (Daffis et al., 2010).

claim: Gibbon and AGM IFIT1B proteins function similarly to mouse IFIT1B, and can specifically inhibit the replication of a virus expressing cap0-mRNAs.
source: Consistent with our yeast assay data, we found that gibbon and AGM IFIT1B proteins function similarly to mouse IFIT1B, and can specifically inhibit the replication of a virus expressing cap0-mRNAs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the vaccinia virus infection experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Human IFIT1B lacks antiviral activity despite being expressed in cell lines.
source: Also consistent with our analyses of IFIT1B in yeast (Figure 4E), human IFIT1B lacks antiviral activity despite being expressed in these cell lines.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the vaccinia virus infection experiments shown in Figure 6D and protein expression data.

claim: Most IFIT1B proteins (except for the putatively non-functional human IFIT1B) share cap0-mRNA recognition as a discriminant of their antiviral function.
source: These results suggest that most IFIT1B proteins (except for the putatively non-functional human IFIT1B) share cap0-mRNA recognition as a discriminant of their antiviral function.
evidence: This is concluded from the vaccinia virus infection experiments shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: Human IFIT1 did not inhibit replication of the vaccinia virus methyltransferase mutant.
source: In contrast to the activity of most IFIT1B proteins, human IFIT1 did not inhibit replication of the vaccinia virus methyltransferase mutant (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the vaccinia virus infection experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Human IFIT1 does not discriminate 'self versus non-self' based on cap0-mRNA versus cap1-mRNA specificity.
source: Consistent with our yeast data, these results demonstrated that human IFIT1 does not discriminate 'self versus non-self' based on cap0-mRNA versus cap1-mRNA specificity.
evidence: This is concluded from the vaccinia virus infection experiments shown in Figure 6C and yeast data in Figure 5.

claim: Neither gibbon nor AGM IFIT1 was able to inhibit the cap0-mRNA expressing vaccinia virus.
source: Likewise, neither gibbon nor AGM IFIT1 was able to inhibit the cap0-mRNA expressing vaccinia virus (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the vaccinia virus infection experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: IFIT1B and IFIT1 lineages evolved to rely on distinct cues for their function.
source: We, therefore, conclude that in keeping with their phylogenetic divergence, IFIT1B and IFIT1 lineages evolved to rely on distinct cues for their function.
evidence: This is concluded from the vaccinia virus infection experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The non-redundancy of IFIT1 and IFIT1B could explain the retention of both genes in most mammalian genomes.
source: Such non-redundancy could explain the retention of both IFIT1 and IFIT1B in most mammalian genomes.
evidence: This is speculated based on the functional data showing distinct specificities of IFIT1 and IFIT1B.

claim: Mouse IFIT1B has no effect on VSV viral titers or virally-encoded GFP expression.
source: As expected, we found that mouse IFIT1B had no effect on either virally-encoded GFP expression (Figure 7A) or viral titers (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the VSV infection experiments shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: VSV viral titers are unaffected by other IFIT1B genes.
source: VSV viral titers were also unaffected by other IFIT1B genes (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the VSV infection experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Human IFIT1 causes a substantial decrease in both VSV viral-GFP expression and viral titer.
source: In contrast, we observed a substantial decrease in both viral-GFP expression and viral titer in cells expressing human IFIT1 (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the VSV infection experiments shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: The inhibitory activity of IFIT1 against VSV is conserved in other primate IFIT1 proteins.
source: This inhibitory activity was also conserved in other primate IFIT1 proteins (Figure 7C), suggesting that multiple IFIT1 proteins are insensitive to cap1-methyltransferase and share the property of inhibiting VSV (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the VSV infection experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Multiple IFIT1 proteins are insensitive to cap1-methyltransferase and share the property of inhibiting VSV.
source: This inhibitory activity was also conserved in other primate IFIT1 proteins (Figure 7C), suggesting that multiple IFIT1 proteins are insensitive to cap1-methyltransferase and share the property of inhibiting VSV (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is concluded from the VSV infection experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: IFIT1B and IFIT1 encode non-redundant antiviral specificities that together expand the antiviral range of the IFIT gene repertoire in mammals.
source: Together with our vaccinia virus data (Figure 6), these data support the conclusion that IFIT1B and IFIT1 encode non-redundant antiviral specificities that together expand the antiviral range of the IFIT gene repertoire in mammals.
evidence: This is concluded from the vaccinia virus and VSV infection experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Gene duplication is a common genetic mechanism of innovation employed by host genomes to escape viral antagonism or evolve new inhibitory mechanisms.
source: One common genetic mechanism of innovation employed by host genomes is gene duplication, which enables hosts to either escape viral antagonism or evolve new inhibitory mechanisms through subfunctionalization.
evidence: This is supported by general knowledge of evolutionary biology.

claim: Many antiviral genes expressed as part of the interferon response represent members of multigene families, whose lineage-specific expansions and contractions have shaped contemporary repertoires of antivirals in mammalian genomes.
source: Indeed, many antiviral genes expressed as part of the interferon response represent members of multigene families, whose lineage-specific expansions and contractions have shaped contemporary repertoires of antivirals in mammalian genomes (Brunette et al., 2012; Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Munk et al., 2012; Tareen et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Brunette et al., 2012; Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Munk et al., 2012; Tareen et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012).

claim: In several multigene families, gene conversion has further diversified the innate immune repertoire of different species.
source: In several of these multigene families, gene conversion has further diversified the innate immune repertoire of different species (Buchmann, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2015; Woelk et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Buchmann, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2015; Woelk et al., 2007).

claim: Every mammalian virus family, except alphaviruses, has evolved a way to produce cap1-mRNAs.
source: However, the general antiviral effectiveness of IFIT1B proteins is limited due to the fact that every mammalian virus family, except alphaviruses, has evolved a way to produce cap1-mRNAs.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of viral biology and citations mentioned elsewhere in the manuscript (Banerjee, 1980; Decroly et al., 2012; Hyde and Diamond, 2015).

claim: Alphaviruses produce cap0-mRNAs.
source: Even in the case of alphaviruses, which produce cap0-mRNAs (Banerjee, 1980) and are therefore predicted to be susceptible to IFIT1B-mediated inhibition, secondary structure changes at the 5' end of alphaviral mRNAs can blunt IFIT1B antiviral action (Hyde et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Banerjee, 1980; Hyde et al., 2014).

claim: Secondary structure changes at the 5' end of alphaviral mRNAs can blunt IFIT1B antiviral action.
source: Even in the case of alphaviruses, which produce cap0-mRNAs (Banerjee, 1980) and are therefore predicted to be susceptible to IFIT1B-mediated inhibition, secondary structure changes at the 5' end of alphaviral mRNAs can blunt IFIT1B antiviral action (Hyde et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Hyde et al., 2014).

claim: The duplication of IFIT1B genes in rodents might have been driven by pressure from alphaviruses or other undiscovered cap0-mRNA expressing viruses.
source: For instance, the duplication of IFIT1B genes in rodents might have been driven by pressure from alphaviruses or other undiscovered cap0-mRNA expressing viruses, and may augment the defenses of rodent hosts against such viruses.
evidence: This is speculated based on the phylogenetic data showing IFIT1B duplication in rodents.

claim: The loss of IFIT1 in many rodents might leave them more susceptible to infection by viruses inhibited by IFIT1, such as VSV.
source: In contrast, the loss of IFIT1 in many rodents might leave them more susceptible to infection by viruses inhibited by IFIT1, such as VSV.
evidence: This is speculated based on the phylogenetic data showing IFIT1 loss in rodents and the functional data showing IFIT1 inhibits VSV.

claim: Loss of IFIT1B function in a broad range of species, including humans, may result in greater ability of cap0-mRNA expressing viruses to replicate in those species.
source: Similarly, loss of IFIT1B function in a broad range of species, including humans, may result in greater ability of cap0-mRNA expressing viruses to replicate in those species.
evidence: This is speculated based on the phylogenetic data showing IFIT1B loss/pseudogenization and the functional data showing IFIT1B inhibits cap0-mRNA viruses.

claim: Rodents may be better prepared than humans, chimpanzees, New World monkeys and several other species to defend against cap0-mRNA expressing viruses such as alphaviruses.
source: In that regard, rodents may be better prepared than humans, chimpanzees, New World monkeys and several other species to defend against cap0-mRNA expressing viruses such as alphaviruses (Figure 3).
evidence: This is speculated based on the phylogenetic data shown in Figure 3 showing rodents have multiple IFIT1B genes while other species have lost IFIT1B.

claim: IFIT gene duplication may be the host's response to the evolutionary arms race where viruses are continually masking their RNAs with 'self' features.
source: Thus, IFIT gene duplication may be the host's response to the evolutionary arms race where viruses are continually masking their RNAs with 'self' features.
evidence: This is speculated based on the evolutionary dynamics of IFIT genes and their functional properties.

claim: When the selective pressure from viruses displaying a given 'non-self' feature has been relaxed, the specific IFIT gene that restricts those viruses may be pseudogenized or lost permanently.
source: On the other hand, when the selective pressure from viruses displaying a given 'non-self' feature (e.g. Cap0-mRNAs) has been relaxed, the specific IFIT gene that restricts those viruses may be pseudogenized or lost permanently.
evidence: This is speculated based on the evolutionary dynamics of IFIT genes.

claim: The dynamic evolution of IFIT genes across mammals will have important consequences for species-specific antiviral immunity.
source: We predict that the dynamic evolution of IFIT genes across mammals will have important consequences for species-specific antiviral immunity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the evolutionary and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: VSV is a virus known to express mRNAs with a cap1-structure.
source: We, therefore, infected our cell lines expressing either human IFIT1 or mouse IFIT1B with vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), a virus known to express mRNAs with a cap1-structure (Ma et al., 2014; Banerjee, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Ma et al., 2014; Banerjee, 1980).

claim: Human IFIT1 inhibits translation of PIV5 2'O-methylated mRNAs.
source: Moreover, human IFIT1 was shown to not just inhibit replication of PIV5, but to inhibit translation of PIV5 2'O-methylated mRNAs (Andrejeva et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Andrejeva et al., 2013).

claim: IFIT2 and IFIT5 have been reported to have sequence- or structure-specific binding to RNA.
source: Supporting this model is the fact that in addition to IFIT1B, IFIT2 and IFIT5 have been reported to have sequence- or structure-specific binding to RNA (Habjan et al., 2013; Katibah et al., 2013; 2014; Yang et al., 2012), suggesting that numerous IFITs may restrict viral replication through recognition of distinct viral RNA patterns.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Habjan et al., 2013; Katibah et al., 2013; 2014; Yang et al., 2012).

claim: Mammalian hosts, as well as vaccinia virus, possess a 'self' molecular pattern to prevent IFIT1-mediated inhibition whereas yeast and VSV display a 'non-self' molecular pattern that cannot block IFIT1 action.
source: Although the presumed molecular pattern that IFIT1 recognizes remains unknown, our data suggest that mammalian hosts, as well as vaccinia virus, possess a 'self' molecular pattern to prevent IFIT1-mediated inhibition whereas yeast and VSV display a 'non-self' molecular pattern that cannot block IFIT1 action.
evidence: This is inferred from the yeast and viral infection data shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Human IFIT1 antiviral activity was previously proposed to result from direct binding and sequestration of 5' triphosphate ends of viral replication intermediates.
source: One previous proposal suggested that human IFIT1 antiviral activity resulted from direct binding and sequestration of 5' triphosphate ends of viral replication intermediates, thus interfering with replication rather than directly inhibiting translation (Pichlmair et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Pichlmair et al., 2011).

claim: IFIT1, like IFIT1B, binds to cap-proximal RNA and prevents binding of mRNAs by the translation initiation factor eIF4F.
source: Biochemical data suggests that IFIT1, like IFIT1B, binds to cap-proximal RNA and prevents binding of mRNAs by the translation initiation factor eIF4F (Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work (Kumar et al., 2014).

claim: The recombination breakpoint falls within the 'pivot' region separating the second and third subdomain of IFIT5 structure.
source: In the structures of IFIT5 bound to the 5' triphosphate containing end of RNA, three 'subdomains' surround the RNA (Abbas et al., 2013). The recombination breakpoint we observed falls within the 'pivot' region separating the second and third subdomain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting the first two subdomains may be important for a common conserved function of IFIT1 and IFIT1B whereas the third subdomain might confer changes to the molecular specificity.
evidence: This is based on structural mapping shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and a citation to previous work (Abbas et al., 2013).

claim: The first two subdomains of IFIT proteins may be important for a common conserved function of IFIT1 and IFIT1B whereas the third subdomain might confer changes to the molecular specificity.
source: The recombination breakpoint we observed falls within the 'pivot' region separating the second and third subdomain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting the first two subdomains may be important for a common conserved function of IFIT1 and IFIT1B whereas the third subdomain might confer changes to the molecular specificity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the location of the recombination breakpoint relative to IFIT5 structure.

claim: The recombination breakpoint occurs just outside of the homooligomerization domain in the structure of IFIT2.
source: We also note that the breakpoint occurs just outside of the homooligomerization domain in the structure of IFIT2 (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on structural mapping shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and a citation to previous work (Yang et al., 2012).

claim: Some IFITs are thought to oligomerize for function.
source: As some IFITs are thought to oligomerize for function (Habjan et al., 2013; Pichlmair et al., 2011), the homogenization of the region corresponding to the oligomerization domain in IFIT2 suggests that IFIT1 and IFIT1B might also need to hetero-oligomerize in species in which both are present.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Habjan et al., 2013; Pichlmair et al., 2011).

claim: IFIT1 and IFIT1B might need to hetero-oligomerize in species in which both are present.
source: As some IFITs are thought to oligomerize for function (Habjan et al., 2013; Pichlmair et al., 2011), the homogenization of the region corresponding to the oligomerization domain in IFIT2 suggests that IFIT1 and IFIT1B might also need to hetero-oligomerize in species in which both are present.
evidence: This is speculated based on the location of the recombination breakpoint and knowledge of IFIT oligomerization.
